case_name: Fox v Scott Safety Supply Services Inc.
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Fox v. Scott Safety Supply Services
Inc.,

2021 BCSC 842

Date: 20210504

Docket:
194391

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Catherine
Fox

Plaintiff

And

Scott
Safety Supply Services Inc.,

Storm Resources Ltd., and Randy Fidler

Defendants

And

Scott Safety Supply Services Inc., Randy Fidler also known as Randy
Fiddler, 312591 Alberta Ltd., doing business as Gerry’s Well Services,

776601 Alberta Ltd., and Storm Resources Ltd.

Third Parties

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Murray

Reasons for Judgment

Plaintiff on her own behalf:

C.
Fox

Counsel for the Defendant, Scott Safety
Supply Services Inc.:

D.
Lucas

Counsel for Storm Resources Ltd.

J. Aiyadurai

Counsel for Third Party, 312591 Alberta
Ltd.

K.
Duffield

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

April
22, 2021

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

May
4, 2021

Introduction

[
1
]

In separate applications heard together, the defendants
Scott Safety Supply Services Inc. (“Scott Safety”) and Storm Resources Ltd.
(“Storm”) seek orders striking the plaintiff’s claims against them on the
grounds of
res judicata
and/or abuse of process pursuant to Rule 9-5 of
the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
. Alternatively, they seek to have the
pleadings dismissed pursuant to Rule 9-6(4) on the ground that there is no
genuine issue for trial with respect to the claims set out in the notice of civil
claim.

[
2
]

By way of brief background, in about September
2017 the plaintiff began working for Scott Safety as a standby medic at a
remote worksite. The worksite was operated by Storm.

[
3
]

In October 2017, the Plaintiff reported
instances of harassment by the defendant Randy Fidler, now deceased, who was
working at the worksite but was not employed by Scott Safety. As a result of
these allegations and as per her request, the plaintiff was moved, within days
of her complaint, to another worksite. She worked two night shifts at the new
site for before the project was completed and the camp shut down. The plaintiff
was not offered further work by Scott Safety.

[
4
]

On April 8, 2018, the plaintiff filed a
complaint against Scott Safety with the Worker’s Compensation Board, WorkSafeBC
(WCB) claiming that, in not offering her further employment, Scott Safety
discriminated against her. She further alleged that Scott Safety failed to pay
wages to her as required.

[
5
]

In a written decision dated November 28, 2018, the
WCB dismissed the plaintiff’s complaint in its entirety. Of import to this
application, the adjudicator found that Scott Safety did not have jobs suitable
for the plaintiff’s level of training available after her work at the second
site ended, and accordingly did not discriminate against the plaintiff.

The Issues

[
6
]

The issue to be decided is whether the notice of
civil claim filed in this court by the plaintiff should be struck and the
action dismissed as against Scott Safety and Storm pursuant to Rule 9-5 or 9-6.

The Law

[
7
]

Rule 9-5 (1) permits the court to strike the
whole or any part of a pleading on the grounds that,
inter alia
:

(a)       it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)       it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious
, or

....

(d)       it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

[
8
]

With
respect to the first ground, Rule 9-5(1)(a), the test is a stringent one: only
if the action, taken as pleaded, is certain to fail should it be struck:
Young
v. Borzoni et al
.,
2007 BCCA 16
at para.
19
.

[
9
]

Regarding Rule 9-5(1)(b), a pleading is
“frivolous” if it is unsustainable due to the issue of estoppel:
Chrisgian
v. BC Rail Ltd. et al
. (6 July 1992), Prince George Registry (BCSC) as
cited in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,

1999 Canlii 5860
at para.
47
.

[
10
]

Issue estoppel, a form of estoppel by res judicata, prevents a party
from re-litigating matters by simply relying upon a different theory of
liability or placing a different “spin” on the same set of facts”:
Rivet v.
British Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 731
at para.
83
.

[
11
]

Issue estoppel can apply to decisions of administrative tribunals:
The
Queen v. Bugbusters Pest Management Inc
.,
1998 Canlii 6467
at para.
19
.

[
12
]

In order for issue estoppel to apply the applicant must satisfy
three requirements:

1)

The same question has been decided in a previous
proceeding;

2)

The earlier decision was final; and

3)

The parties, or their privies, were the same in
both proceedings.

See
British Columbia (Workers’
Compensation Board) v. Figliola
,
2011 SCC 52
at para.
27
.

[
13
]

The following sections of the
Workers
Compensation Act
, RSBC 1996, c. 492 (
WCA
), which applies to this
proceeding, are pertinent to the second requirement:

10
(1)   The
provisions of this Part are in lieu of any right and rights of action, statutory
or otherwise, founded on a breach of duty of care or any other cause of action,
whether that duty or cause of action is imposed by or arises by reason of law
or contract, express or implied, to which a worker, dependant or member of the
family of the worker is or may be entitled against the employer of the worker,
or against any employer within the scope of this Part, or against any worker,
in respect of any personal injury, disablement or death arising out of and in
the course of employment and no action in respect of it lies. This provision
applies only when the action or conduct of the employer, the employer's servant
or agent, or the worker, which caused the breach of duty arose out of and in
the course of employment within the scope of this Part.

….

96
(1)   Subject
to sections 239 and 240, the Board has exclusive jurisdiction to inquire into,
hear and determine all matters and questions of fact and law arising under this
Part, and the action or decision of the Board on them is final and conclusive
and is not open to question or review in any court, and proceedings by or
before the Board must not be restrained by injunction, prohibition or other
process or proceeding in any court or be removable by certiorari or otherwise
into any court, and an action may not be maintained or brought against the
Board or a director, an officer, or an employee of the Board in respect of any
act, omission or decision that was within the jurisdiction of the Board or that
the Board, director, officer or employee believed was within the jurisdiction
of the Board; and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, the
Board has exclusive jurisdiction to inquire into, hear and determine

(a)        the
question whether an injury has arisen out of or in the course of an employment
within the scope of this Part;

(b)        the
existence and degree of disability by reason of an injury;

…

(d)        the
degree of diminution of earning capacity by reason of an injury;

….

[
14
]

I take from those sections that:

1)

The matters in issue in the plaintiff’s actions
in this court are within the exclusive jurisdiction of WSBC: s. 10(1);

2)

The rulings of WCB are final and conclusive: s. 96(1).

[
15
]

The procedure for review or appeal a decision of the WCB is provided
for in the
WCA
as well. Pursuant to
ss. 96.2
to
96.5

WCA
, a
directly affected person may request a review by a review officer and pursuant
to s. 239, a decision of the reviewing officer may be appealed to the Workers’
Compensation Appeal Tribunal (appeal tribunal).

[
16
]

Of note, sections 254 and 255 provide that the
appeal tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to hear appeals from review
officer’s or Board decisions and that appeal tribunal decisions are final and
conclusive and not open to question or review in any court:

254      The
appeal tribunal has
exclusive jurisdiction
to inquire into, hear and
determine all those matters and questions of fact, law and discretion arising
or required to be determined under this Part and to make any order permitted to
be made, including the following:

(a)        all appeals from review
officers' decisions as permitted under section 239;

(b)        all appeals from Board decisions
or orders as permitted under section 240;

(c)        all matters that the appeal
tribunal is requested to determine under section 257;

(d)        all other matters for which the
Lieutenant Governor in Council by regulation permits an appeal to the appeal
tribunal under this Part.

255      (1)        Any
decision or action of the chair or the appeal tribunal under this Part
is
final and conclusive and is not open to question or review in any court
.

(2)        Proceedings by or before the
chair or appeal tribunal under this Part must not

(a)        be restrained by injunction, prohibition
or other process or proceeding in any court, or

(b)        be removed by certiorari or
otherwise into any court.

(3)        The Board must comply with a
final decision of the appeal tribunal made in an appeal under this Part.

(4)        A party in whose favour the appeal
tribunal makes a final decision, or a person designated in the final decision,
may file a certified copy of the final decision with the Supreme Court.

(5)
A final decision filed under
subsection (4) has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken
on it, as if it were a judgment of the Supreme Court
.

[Emphasis added.]

[
17
]

All decisions of the Board and appeal tribunal are subject to
judicial review.

[
18
]

Finally, regarding Rule 9-5(1)(d), it is an
abuse of process to use a civil action to challenge the decision of a tribunal.
As stated by Joyce, J. in
Stephen v. Her Majesty the Queen,

2008 BCSC
1656
:

[51]      In determining whether proceedings
constitute an abuse of process, the court may consider whether there have been
multiple or successive related proceedings that are likely to cause vexation or
oppression.
In particular, it is an abuse of court process to use a civil
action to collaterally challenge decisions of an administrative tribunal that
are otherwise subject to a statutory right of appeal or review
:
Borzoni

at
paras.
65-66
;
Gemex Developments Corp. v. Coquitlam (City)
,
2002 BCSC
412
;
Varzeliotis (c.o.b.) v. British Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 620
.

[Emphasis
added.]

See also
Cimaco
International Sales, Inc. v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
2010 BCCA
342
at paras.
56-57
.

[
19
]

With that law in mind, I turn to analyze the issues.

Analysis

[
20
]

In her civil action the plaintiff seeks damages for constructive and
wrongful dismissal and personal injury. Scott Safety submits that these are the
same claims that were before the WCB. It further submits that as the decisions
of the WCB are final and conclusive as they have not been overturned on appeal
or through judicial review, the issues have already been decided. Accordingly, it
would be an abuse of process to allow this civil claim to proceed on the basis
of
res judicata
.

[
21
]

Similarly, Storm takes the position that the issues have already
been determined by the WCB and argues that
s. 10(1)

WCA
is a complete
bar to bringing this action against either Scott Safety or Storm. As such says
Storm, the plaintiff’s action is an abuse of process.

[
22
]

The plaintiff argues that she is not trying to re-litigate the
issues before the WCB. She stresses that her civil action is for wrongful
dismissal.

[
23
]

I agree with Scott Safety and Storm. The issues raised in the civil
action have been decided by the WCB. Those decisions are final. The plaintiff’s
recourse was through the appeal processes set out in the
WCA
or through
judicial review. To allow the plaintiff to re-litigate the issues by putting a
different spin on them would be an abuse of process.

[
24
]

Having reached this conclusion, there is no need to address the
other arguments. However, for completeness I am satisfied that the issue of
res
judicata
applies to the action again Scott Safety. I am further satisfied
that
s. 10(1)

WCA
is a complete bar to bringing this action against both
Scott Safety and Storm.

[
25
]

Accordingly, I order that the pleadings against Scott Safety and
Storm be struck and the proceedings against them dismissed.

Conclusion

[
26
]

I make the following orders:

1)

The pleadings against Scott Safety and Storm are
struck and the actions against them are dismissed;

2)

The signature of the plaintiff on the order is
dispensed with.

“The
Honourable Madam Justice Murray”
